Proposed Variation No1 of Clare County 
Development Plan 2023-2029 
The Proposed Variation No. 1 of the Clare County Development 
Plan 2023-2029 has been prepared and went on public display 
from 6th March 2026. The final date for display and submissions 
will be 7th April 2026.
The reason for the proposed variation is to give effect to the 
Ministerial Guidelines on NPF Implementation: Housing Growth 
Requirements, published on 29th July 2025 (https://www.gov.
ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/
publications/section-28-guidelines-npf-implementation-
housing-growth-requirements/). The Guidelines contain a 
requirement that Development Plans are updated in line with 
accelerated annual Housing Unit Targets for each Planning 
Authority. Those targets reflect the requirements of the Revised 
National Planning Framework (NPF) (issued April 2025) in 
which a significant acceleration in housing delivery is identified 
for implementation nationally. The Guidelines provide for an 
increased annual housing growth requirement for Clare County 
Council, and an ‘additional provision’ mechanism to support the 
zoning of additional lands in areas where it can be justified.
In total, the proposed Variation includes newly-identified 
Residential zoning at 67 sites across 25 settlements and across all 
4 Municipal Districts. It also facilitates the positive assessment, in 
principle, of Residential development applications immediately 
upon adoption of the proposed Variation, by changing Strategic 
Residential Reserve lands to Residential zoning. This accounts for 
87 sites at 29 settlements, again across all 4 Municipal Districts.
The proposed Variation also facilitates the small number of 
instances where it is necessary to change the zoning of lands (in 
the County Development Plan) in accordance with the Finance 
Act 2021, as amended by the Finance Act 2024, and the policy 
and guidance in the Residential Zoned Land Tax - Change in 
zoning of land subject to existing economic activity Guidelines for 
Planning Authorities (2024). 
The incorporation into the County Development Plan 2023-2029 
of the ‘Ennis 2040 Economic and Spatial Strategy’ is provided for 
in the proposed Variation, as is the incorporation of ‘Ennis Local 
Transport Plan’. Upon adoption of the proposed Variation, both 
of these documents will form individual volumes of the Plan. 
The inclusion of both documents will help to optimise the future 
patterns of land-use zoning in the Ennis Municipal District and 
support significant acceleration in housing delivery.

Marine Spatial Planning
Last year the Government’s Marine Environment functions 
and responsibilities transferred to the Department of Climate, 
Energy, and the Environment (DCEE), consolidating several 
maritime functions under one Department. Following initiation 
of the €25m Marine Protected Area (MPA) Life Ireland project 
coordinated by the Department, the Department together with 
the MPA LIFE team and the MPA Advisory Group, has commenced 
a new Ecological Sensitivity Analysis project for Irelands Atlantic 
waters running throughout 2026. The study will assess marine 
ecological features that may warrant area-based protection and 
will help identify future MPA locations.
This new project builds on previous analyses carried out for the 
western Irish sea and Celtic Sea between 2022 and 2024 and 
will operate in parallel with the National DMAP process (DMAP 
- Designated Marine Area Plan) for offshore renewable energy 
to ensure full alignment. It is co-chaired by Prof. Tasman Crowe 
(UCD) and Prof Louise Allcock (University of Galway).
The MPA LIFE Ireland project is aimed at significantly expanding 
Ireland’s network of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) to reach a

Its core goal is to make a major contribution to protecting,

ecosystems, thereby supporting the achievement of Good 
Environmental Status in our marine environment.
Operationally, the project will examine and develop area-based 
conservation measures for a wide range of vulnerable species, 
habitats, and other sensitive features that need protection based 
on current knowledge and scientific evidence.
These measures in the form of MPAs, along with their conservation 
objectives and management plans, will be developed and 
delivered with the active engagement and participation of 
stakeholders and citizens. This will ensure a robust and meaningful 
process for the designation and management of MPAs in Ireland.
The MPA LIFE project is set to span nine years up to 2033, and 
is a partnership between the Department of Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage, University College Dublin, University 
College Cork and the University of Galway.
The project is jointly funded by the Department of Housing, 
Local Government and Heritage and the European Union’s LIFE 
programme.

In general terms, MPAs can be considered to be geographically 
defined maritime areas that provide levels of protection to 
achieve conservation objectives.
MPAs can support economic activity associated with the sea; 
for example, by conserving areas of particular importance to 
marine ecosystems and ensuring that human activity is kept at 
a level that will sustain biological diversity, natural productivity, 
human health and well-being. MPAs can also help reduce the 
effects of climate change and ocean acidification by ensuring that 
marine ecosystems are healthy and resilient, and that the marine 
environment can act as a natural carbon storage system.

Archaeology Workshop at Clare County Council
A workshop on Archaeology took place at Clare County Council 
where John Olney and Hugh Carey, Archaeologists from 
the Department’s Development Applications Unit, National 
Monuments Services (NMS), Department of Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage made a presentation to Planners on 
the process of Planning Applications involving Archaeology. 
John Olney gave a PowerPoint presentation setting out the role 
of NMS in the planning process, legislative background, context 
and criteria for referral of planning applications to NMS and the 
use of GIS. Case studies and examples were used for illustration, 
followed by Q&A, an exchange of information, feedback and 
discussion.

Launch of the Clare’s Stained Glass Archive
Clare’s Stained Glass Archive is an extensive online archive, 
which was created by West Clare–based researcher and 
photographer John Glynn. This archive brings together over five 
years of research into stained glass windows from more than 130 
religious and secular sites throughout County Clare. The project 
highlights a significant yet often under‑recognised aspect of 
Clare’s cultural heritage, spanning seven centuries from the 14th 
century to the present day. The archive documents over 1,000 
images of stained-glass windows and their buildings, alongside 
detailed information including location, art, architectural and 
historical context, including the artists and studios involved such 
as Harry Clarke Studios and Clare native Catherine O’Brien. On 
Clareheritage.org each window has its own description and high-
quality image with a summary of its title, location, inscriptions 
and donors. The archive also includes Bunratty Castle, home to 
over 100 medieval and pre‑19th‑century stained glass windows 
sourced from England, Switzerland, Germany and the Benelux 
region.

BIODIVERSITY
Launch of the Clare County Biodiversity Action Plan 
2025-2031
Tuesday, 3rd of March 2026, marked the launch of the Clare 
County Biodiversity Action Plan 2025-2031 on World Wildlife 
Day. The launch event took place at the Michael Cusack Heritage 
Centre located in Carran, in the Burren. The Clare County 
Biodiversity Action Plan 2025-2031 sets out a clear and ambitious 
framework for biodiversity action over the next six years with the 
overall aim to halt biodiversity loss and drive nature recovery 
within the county. Speakers included Cathaoirleach of Clare 
County Council, Cllr Paul Murphy, Chief Executive Gordon Daly, 
Dr Martina Moloney (Chairperson of the Heritage Council), Barry 
O’Loughlin (Biodiversity Officer), Dr. Catherine Farrell (TCD), 
Jennie Drysdale (Doonbeg Tidy Towns), Elaine Bradley (Irish Seed 
Savers) and Phoebe O’Brien (Botanist). The new plan outlines a 
vision supported by five key pillars, five overarching objectives, 
fifty-eight actions and associated targets and Key Performance 
Indicators (KPIs). The plan is underpinned by Ireland’s 4th National 
Biodiversity Action Plan 2023-2030 and aligns with the strategic 
biodiversity objectives of the Clare County Development Plan 
2023-2029. The Local Authority Biodiversity Officer Programme 
is delivered in Partnership with the Heritage Council. 
The plan is available to download at the link: https://www.
clarecoco.ie/sites/default/files/2026-03/Clare%20County%20
Biodiversity%20Action%20Plan%202025-2031.pdf

Rural Regeneration and Development Fund (RRDF) 
2026
Minister Dara Calleary TD officially opened the Category 1 call 
for proposals under the Rural Regeneration and Development 
Fund (RRDF) on 27 February 2026. This is the latest call in the 
long-running €1 billion national rural investment programme 
delivered under Project Ireland 2040, Our Rural Future and the 
Town Centre First policy.
This Call invites applications for large-scale capital projects that 
can deliver significant regeneration and development in rural 
towns and villages across Ireland. 
Eligible projects must be “ready to commence” - meaning they 
have all necessary consents and planning in place and can move 
quickly to delivery. 
Projects must demonstrate collaboration between at least two 
partners; clear community engagement and alignment with 
local/regional strategies (e.g. Town Centre First plans, County 
Development Plans)
•	
Minimum funding request: €500,000. 
•	
Maximum funding request: €10 million. 
Each local authority may submit a maximum of two applications, 
with funding of up to €10 million available for one project and up 
to €5 million for a second project.
Closing date for Category 1 submissions is 12 pm on Tuesday, 
28 July 2026.

CLAR Projects 2024
Three community-focused projects below have recently been 
complete with assistance from the 2024 CLAR Scheme. Each 
project received funding of €50,000. These projects were 
designed to enhance community infrastructure, and improve 
safety and accessibility
1.	 St Senan’s GAA - Parking upgrade and Fencing Works
Funding: €50,000
This project delivered essential infrastructure upgrades to 
improve safety, accessibility, and overall usability of the club 
grounds. Works completed included the repair and upgrade of car 
parking facilities and entrance area along with the enhancement 
of the perimeter walking/running track, including boundary and 
safety improvements.
The improvements have enhanced the appearance and 
functionality of the facilities and will promote increased 
community use while ensuring the grounds are safe and fit for 
purpose for all users.
2.	 Scoil Realt na Mara - Astro Turf and Sensory Garden
Funding: €50,000
Scoil Realt na Mara National School is located in Kilkee, Co. 
Clare. The school identified a need to enhance the usability and 
inclusivity of its outdoor space, particularly for recreational and 
sensory development activities. 
Key Works carried out include the installation of a weather-
resistant astro-turf play surface; the development of an inclusive 
sensory garden to support emotional and sensory needs; 
planting of native pollinator species to promote biodiversity and 
environmental learning and the installation of perimeter fencing 
and controlled access points to enhance safety and security.
The project has transformed the previously underutilised 
grounds into a safe, inclusive, and multifunctional outdoor 
space that supports physical activity, sensory development, and 
environmental education.
 
3.	 Broadford GAA - Car Park
Funding: €50,000
Broadford village has experienced significant challenges with 
car parking availability in the village. Existing parking facilities, 
including those provided by the local GAA grounds, were 
insufficient - especially during high-demand periods such as 
match days, training sessions, and school drop-off and collection 
times. Local businesses on the main street have also been affected 
by limited parking, which has restricted access for customers and 
deliveries.
The aim of the project was to address the shortage of parking 
in Broadford village by developing a dedicated car parking area 
at the site of the new Astro Turf facility. The project addressed 
a critical infrastructure gap within the village, supporting 
community activities, local services, and economic activity

Women In Sport Week 2026
The Clare Sports Partnership and Clare County Council promoted 
Women in Sport Week 2026 which ran from 2-9 March 
culminating in International Women’s Day on 8th March. The 
main aim of Women in Sport Week is to celebrate every woman 
and girl who plays, coaches, officiates, volunteers, leads or works 
in sport. 
The theme of Women in Sport Week this year was “Same Energy”. 
While significant progress has been made in recent years, 
women’s sport is still too often met with less anticipation, less 
media coverage, and less cultural importance than men’s sport. 
Same Energy challenges us to ask whether we’re bringing the 
same energy, excitement, commitment and visibility to women’s

Carer’s Appreciation Day - 13th March 2026
Clare Age Friendly Programme and the HSE collaborated to 
deliver a pilot Carers Appreciation Day on the 13th of March 2026, 
dedicated to recognising and supporting home care workers. The 
aim of the event was to provide home support staff with essential 
tools, knowledge, and wellbeing resources to strengthen their 
ability to care for others within their communities. The day 
emphasised self‑care, professional development, and access to 
local supports.
The event opened with registration and information stands, 
offering attendees an opportunity to meet service providers from 
across the county. This was followed by warm welcoming remarks 
from Master of Ceremonies, Ciana Campbell, and Cllr. Mary 
Howard, Leas Cathaoirleach, who acknowledged the invaluable 
contribution home care workers make every day.
A strong and varied line-up of speakers delivered engaging and 
practical sessions throughout the morning.
•	
Lourda Bermingham, Home Care Package Co‑ordinator, 
outlined supports available through Community Services for 
Older People.
•	
Emma Lynch, Career Coach specialising in burnout, spoke 
about maintaining balance, boundaries, and resilience in 
caring roles.
•	
John Carey and Jamie Fitzgibbon from Active Ennis 
highlighted the importance of physical wellbeing and 
demonstrated accessible movement and fitness options.
•	
Cillian Keane of Mental Health Ireland offered guidance 
on maintaining mental health and recognising early signs of 
stress.
•	
Sharon Meaney from the Clare Volunteer Centre discussed 
community involvement and volunteer supports available 
across the county.
•	
Mindfulness Practitioner Fergus Barrett closed the speaker 
sessions with calming techniques to help staff ground 
themselves during demanding workdays.
Home care workers enjoyed a served lunch, a performance by 
the choir, and time to engage with a wide range of stallholders. 
Exhibitors included Clare Local Safety Partnership, Cultural 
Companions, Croí, Samaritans, Alzheimer Society of Clare, 
Shannon Estuary Way Retreats, Flow Holistic Care, Mental Health 
Ireland, Active Ennis, and the HSE Quit Smoking and Cancer 
Prevention Teams. Each organisation provided information, 
resources, and practical advice relevant to the wellbeing of carers.
To further encourage rest and relaxation, attendees were offered 
taster self‑care sessions delivered by Anne McAuliffe (RGN, RM), 
Talamh Holistics, Rachel Nagle (Reflexology/Elm Wellness), Laura 
McAuliffe (Draíocht Healing), Gillian McMahon (Flow Holistic 
Care), and Samantha McCarthy (Sam’s Yoga). These sessions gave 
carers the chance to experience holistic supports first‑hand.
Overall, the pilot event created a meaningful and uplifting space 
for home care workers to recharge, learn, and feel valued, while 
strengthening their capacity to support older people across their 
communities.

Provision and Land Activation Directorate and the key objective 
being to bring together our resources with a strong ambition for 
delivery of increased activation of vacant and derelict properties 
throughout the County. The Property Management unit deals 
with the Council owned lands and properties.
Working collaboratively across the other units in the Directorate 
with pooled resources and knowledge, it is intended to increase 
levels of activity and engagement to activate more properties for 
delivery of housing, both public and private.
Taking action on dereliction and vacancy is a priority in the 
National Housing Plan 2025, with the re-use and regeneration 
of vacant and derelict properties in cities, towns and villages 
providing much needed housing and transforming and revitalizing 
communities, as summarised hereunder.
 
DERELICT SITES
A significant effort to transform the many derelict properties 
across the County is underway with 354 derelict 
properties being dealt with by the Derelict Sites Team as of 
the 20th March 2026. A further 25 properties have been identified 
for action in the last month. The team maintains very high levels 
of activity and engagement with owners and their legal/technical 
representatives. This initial engagement is key to resolution of 
the issues of dereliction and to gain an understanding of the 
various reasons why the properties are in a derelict state. Where 
derelict properties are sold by the owner, the Derelict Sites Team 
engages promptly with the new owners to brief them on their 
responsibilities under the Derelict Sites Act, 1990. 
To bolster the momentum, the Council is advising property 
owners on accessing the vacant property refurbishment grant. 
The Team is also seeing a consistent number of planning 
applications for property refurbishment/extensions, and it is 
clear from driving around the county the level of work ongoing 
on individual properties. The Derelict Sites Team believe that by 
working in partnership with owners and financial institutions,

Driving positive change - transforming dereliction 
Revitalising vacant and neglected properties is about far more 
than cosmetic improvements - it’s about unlocking the full 
potential of our communities. Clare County Council’s Derelict Sites 
Section is driving this transformation with energy, determination, 
and a strong commitment to using the Derelict Sites Act 1990 to 
its fullest effect.
Derelict buildings have negatively impacted the character and 
vibrancy of our towns, villages and rural hinterlands. Through a 
focused, proactive, and systematic approach, we are changing 
that. Our team is significantly expanding the number of properties 
we are actively progressing under the legislation - rising from 303 
at the end of 2025 to 354 today - and ensuring every available 
legal tool is put to work.
This focussed effort is helping to restore community pride and 
bring valuable properties - especially homes - back into productive 
use. It builds on the hard work done to date in rejuvenating 
communities across County Clare and creating places where 
people are proud to live and work and enjoy.
A Call to Action for Property Owners
The Derelict Sites Section is here to support and guide property 
owners in identifying solutions, accessing available schemes, 
and navigating the steps needed to bring properties back into 
habitable use. However, the provisions of the Derelict Sites Act 
1990 will be applied which may result in the property being placed 
on the Derelict Sites Register, application of 7% levy and/or CPO. 
By taking immediate early action - whether through restoration 
or exploring reuse options - owners can help minimise the levy 
amounts payable and contribute to the overall wellbeing and 
appearance of their community.

of 7% of the value of the property, with accruing interest of
